label: CFISD 2026–2027 High School Course Description Handbook

reminders.text: Algebra II is NOT required to graduate, but IS required for Distinguished Level of Achievement and automatic college admission eligibility.
FAFSA or TAFSA must be completed before receiving a diploma (parents can opt out in writing; students 18+ can opt themselves out).
Course change requests must be submitted by the last day of April. No changes after the 2nd week of each semester.
NEW for Class of 2030+: A 5-column GPA scale adds an 'Advanced' (K-level) tier — AP/Dual Credit A=7, K-level A=6.5, On-Level A=6.
To enter K-level (Academic Advanced) or AP for the first time, you need an 85+ yearly average in the previous on-level class OR Masters on STAAR/EOC, plus parent permission.
NEW in 2026–27: CFISD Virtual Pathways launches — Virtual Academy (fully online), Flex Learning (hybrid for 11th–12th), and Supplemental Courses (tuition-based, outside school day).
Class of 2030+ Social Studies change: Personal Financial Literacy (½ credit) replaces Economics (½ credit); Economics becomes an option for the first SS requirement.
Honor designations: Summa cum laude = 6.5 GPA | Magna cum laude = 6.25 GPA | Cum laude = 6.0 GPA.

graduationReqs.subject: PACE / PACE Plus
graduationReqs.note: Required in Grade 9. CPR embedded in PACE. PACE Plus (1 credit) for students who did not pass all 8th-grade core classes or didn't meet STAAR standards.

graduationReqs.subject: Mathematics
graduationReqs.note: Algebra I, Geometry + 1 additional; +1 advanced math for endorsement. Algebra II required for Distinguished Level of Achievement.

graduationReqs.subject: Science
graduationReqs.note: Biology + IPC, Chemistry, or Physics + 1 additional; +1 advanced science for endorsement.

graduationReqs.subject: Social Studies
graduationReqs.note: Classes 2018–2029: World Geo or World History, U.S. History, Gov't (½), Economics (½). Class of 2030+: World Geo/History/Economics, U.S. History, Gov't (½), Personal Financial Literacy (½).

graduationReqs.subject: Languages Other Than English
graduationReqs.note: Two credits in the same language. Computer Science I K or CS II K also satisfies LOTE.

graduationReqs.subject: Physical Education
graduationReqs.note: Max 2 PE credits toward graduation. Alternatives: marching band, cheerleading (fall), drill team, athletics, AFJROTC, district-approved off-campus training.

graduationReqs.subject: Fine Arts
graduationReqs.note: Art, music, dance, theatre, or floral design. Must take 2 sequential semesters of the same course.

graduationReqs.subject: Health
graduationReqs.note: Required through Class of 2028. Any grade, or via correspondence/summer/CBE. Principles of Health Science satisfies this. CPR embedded in Health.

graduationReqs.subject: Electives
graduationReqs.note: +2 additional elective credits for endorsement completion.

endorsements.name: STEM
endorsements.subtitle: Science · Technology · Engineering · Math
endorsements.bestFor: Students who love coding, engineering, advanced math, research, or lab science.

routes.name: Option 1: Computer Science
routes.desc: 4 CS courses: CS I K or Advanced, AP Computer Science Principles, CS II K or Advanced, CS III K or Advanced, CS IV K or Advanced

routes.name: Option 2: CTE Engineering
routes.desc: 4 CTE credits, at least 2 courses in same STEM cluster, with at least 1 advanced CTE course (3rd year or higher)

routes.name: Option 3: Math
routes.desc: Algebra I + Geometry + Algebra II + 2 courses for which Algebra II is a prerequisite: Pre-Calculus, Calculus AB/BC, AP Statistics, AQR K/Advanced, Advanced Algebra, or College Algebra K/Advanced

routes.name: Option 4: Science
routes.desc: Biology + Chemistry + Physics + 2 of: AP Chemistry, AP Biology, Anatomy & Physiology, AP Environmental Science, AP Physics I/II/C, Aquatic Science, Astronomy, Earth & Space Science, Environmental Systems, Forensic Science, Engineering Design & Problem Solving, Advanced Animal/Plant Science, Pathophysiology

routes.name: Option 5: Combination
routes.desc: Algebra II + Chemistry + Physics + 1 additional math + 1 additional science + 3 credits from Option 1 (CS) and/or Option 2 (CTE). At least 1 CTE course must be advanced if CTE is included.

endorsements.name: Business & Industry
endorsements.subtitle: Business · Media · Tech · Trades
endorsements.bestFor: Students interested in entrepreneurship, media production, IT, architecture, or skilled trades.

routes.name: Option 1: CTE Sequence
routes.desc: 4 credits in an approved cluster (Ag, Architecture, Arts/A-V, Business, Hospitality, IT, Manufacturing, Transportation) with at least 1 advanced course

routes.name: Option 2: Journalism/Debate
routes.desc: 4 English elective credits including 3 levels in Advanced Journalism (Newspaper or Yearbook) or Debate

routes.name: Option 3: Combination
routes.desc: Coherent 4-credit sequence from Options 1 and 2 with at least 1 advanced CTE course

endorsements.name: Public Services
endorsements.subtitle: Healthcare · Education · Service
endorsements.bestFor: Students interested in healthcare, teaching, counseling, social work, or military leadership.

routes.name: Option 1: CTE (Health Science, Education, Human Services)
routes.desc: 4 credits in Education & Training, Health Science, or Human Services cluster, with at least 1 advanced course (3rd year or higher)

endorsements.name: Arts & Humanities
endorsements.subtitle: Art · Music · Theatre · Languages · Culture
endorsements.bestFor: Students who love creative expression, world cultures, languages, history, and storytelling.

routes.name: Option 2: Languages
routes.desc: 4 levels of the same foreign language, OR 2 levels each in 2 different foreign languages (4 credits total)

routes.name: Option 3: Fine Arts
routes.desc: 4 courses in the same fine arts area for 4 credits, OR 2 courses in one fine arts area + 2 courses in a different fine arts area

endorsements.name: Multidisciplinary Studies
endorsements.subtitle: Broad College-Prep Path
endorsements.bestFor: Students who want a well-rounded, rigorous college-prep program without specializing in one area.

routes.name: Option 1: Four by Four (4×4)
routes.desc: 4 English credits (including English IV) + 4 Math credits + 4 Science credits (Biology + Chemistry and/or Physics) + 4 Social Studies credits

routes.name: Option 2: AP / Dual Credit
routes.desc: 4 Advanced Placement (AP) or 4 Dual Credit courses, or a combination totaling 4 credits in English, math, science, social studies, foreign language, or fine arts

careers: Any field — keeps all doors open

handbookQA.answer: You need 26 total credits to graduate under the Foundation + Endorsement plan: 22 Foundation credits plus 4 endorsement credits (1 advanced math, 1 advanced science, 2 additional electives). Without an endorsement the minimum is 22 credits, but you won't receive an endorsement designation on your diploma.

One year of coursework earns 1 Carnegie credit per course. CFISD high schools run on a semester system with 7 classes per day, so you can earn up to 7 credits per regular school year. Additional credits can be earned through summer school, correspondence, credit-by-exam, Virtual Pathways, or dual credit college courses.

You must complete 4 English credits — English I, II, III, and IV — taken in sequence. K-level, AP, and Dual Credit versions are available. Dual Credit English III requires passing the English II EOC assessment before enrolling.

You need 3 math credits for the Foundation plan: Algebra I, Geometry, and one additional math course. The endorsement adds 1 more advanced math credit (4 total). Algebra II is not required to graduate but IS required for the Distinguished Level of Achievement and college automatic admission.

Algebra II is NOT required to graduate under the Foundation plan. However, without Algebra II you cannot earn the Distinguished Level of Achievement, which means you won't qualify for automatic college admission (top 10% rule) or the TEXAS Grant and Texas Educational Opportunity Grant financial aid programs. Most college-bound students should take it.

You need 3 science credits: Biology (required for all students), plus IPC, Chemistry, or Physics, plus one additional science. The endorsement adds 1 more advanced science credit (4 total). Biology is the only state-mandated specific science course.

You need 3 social studies credits. Classes of 2018–2029: World Geography or World History, U.S. History, Government (½ credit), and Economics (½ credit). Class of 2030 and beyond: World Geography, World History, or Economics (choose one), U.S. History, Government (½ credit), and Personal Financial Literacy (½ credit). AP Human Geography may substitute for World Geography.

Starting with the Class of 2030 (entering 9th grade Fall 2026+), Personal Financial Literacy (½ credit) replaces Economics (½ credit) as a graduation requirement. Economics itself becomes one of three options for the first social studies requirement alongside World Geography and World History. AP Economics may substitute for Personal Financial Literacy.

You need 2 credits in the same foreign language (e.g., Spanish I and Spanish II). The two credits must be in the same language — you cannot mix Spanish I and French I. Computer Science I K also satisfies the LOTE graduation requirement as an alternative.

Yes — Computer Science I K (and Computer Science II K) satisfies the LOTE (Language Other Than English) graduation requirement. This is a popular option for students in the STEM endorsement pathway who want to use CS credits toward their foreign language requirement.

You need 1 PE credit to graduate. Starting Fall 2022, only 2 PE credits maximum count toward graduation. You can satisfy PE through: marching band (fall semester), cheerleading (fall semester), drill team (both semesters), athletics, AFJROTC, or a district-approved Olympic-caliber off-campus training program. Up to 4 PE credits can be earned through off-campus PE, athletics, or AFJROTC, though only 2 count toward graduation.

You need 1 fine arts credit. Approved options include art, music, dance, theatre, and floral design. You must take 2 sequential semesters of the SAME course — for example, Art I fall and Art I spring. You cannot combine two different fine arts courses to satisfy this requirement.

Health (½ credit) is required for graduation through the Class of 2028. It can be taken in any grade or through correspondence, summer school, or credit-by-exam. Completing Principles of Health Science satisfies the health requirement. CPR instruction is embedded in Health class as a state requirement.

PACE (Personal, Academic & Career Exploration) is required for ALL 9th graders and earns ½ credit. PACE Plus (1 credit) is required instead for students who did not pass all 8th-grade core academic classes or did not meet STAAR state standards. Both PACE and PACE Plus embed the state-required Speech TEKS and CPR instruction.

keywords: do i have to file fafsa
handbookQA.answer: Completing FAFSA or TAFSA is a graduation requirement — you cannot receive your diploma without it. A parent or legal guardian may submit written notice to opt out on your behalf. Students who are at least 18 years old may opt themselves out in writing. The opt-out must be submitted proactively; it does not happen automatically.

The Foundation plan requires 4.5 elective credits. The endorsement adds 2 more, for 6.5 elective credits total. These electives are where you build your endorsement pathway — CTE sequences, additional CS courses, journalism, etc.

The Distinguished Level of Achievement requires completing the Foundation + Endorsement plan AND including Algebra II. It qualifies you for automatic college admission (top 10% rule), TEXAS Grant Program, and Texas Educational Opportunity Grant. Without Algebra II, you lose all three of these benefits even if you graduate with an endorsement.

Students in the top 10% of their graduating class from an accredited Texas school are automatically admitted to Texas public universities if they: completed the Distinguished Level of Achievement, met college readiness standards on ACT/SAT, submitted their application before deadlines, and met curriculum requirements. Note: UT Austin may cap the number admitted under this rule and may admit to the university but not a specific college within it.

keywords: k level for the first time
handbookQA.answer: First-time entry into K-level (Academic Advanced) or AP requires ONE of: (1) 85+ yearly average in the previous on-level class in the same subject, OR (2) Masters Grade Level on STAAR (9th graders) or on the End-of-Course exam (10th–12th graders) for that subject. Parent permission is also required. Students already in K-level can continue if they earned a 75+ second-semester average.

Earning Masters Grade Level on STAAR or an End-of-Course (EOC) assessment qualifies you for first-time entry into K-level or AP without needing an 85 average. For example: Masters on 8th-grade Science STAAR qualifies for Biology Advanced; Masters on English I EOC qualifies for K-level English II; Masters on Algebra EOC qualifies for K-level Geometry or Geometry Advanced.
handbookQA.source: First Time K-level Eligibility through STAAR/EOC (p. 13–14)

keywords: what happens if i fail ap
handbookQA.answer: If you earn a semester average of 74 or lower in a K-level or AP class, you will be moved to an on-level class the following semester (if available). If you earn 69 or lower in any single grading period, you may be moved immediately for the rest of the year. No grade adjustments are made to semester averages when you're removed.

keywords: can i choose to leave ap
handbookQA.answer: You can voluntarily request to drop a K-level or Academic Advanced class with parent approval at the end of any grading period. If your average falls below 80 at the 3rd week, 6th week, or any grading period in a K-level class, you (with parent approval) may request a move to on-level for the rest of the year. If dropping from AP, you may move to K-level, Academic Advanced, or on-level. No grade adjustment when dropping from AP to K-level.

keywords: drop from k to l level grade change
handbookQA.answer: When you move from a K-level or Academic Advanced class to an on-level class, grade adjustment points are added to your current 3-week average or final average in the 1st and 3rd grading periods only. No adjustment is made to semester averages, to grades earned in previous grading periods, or to failing grades (a failing grade won't be bumped above 69). Adjustments are also not made to grades of B or higher.

To qualify for dual credit you must meet ONE academic criterion: 85+ yearly average in the previous on-level course in that subject, OR 75+ second-semester average in the previous K-level course in that subject, OR Masters Grade Level on STAAR/EOC. You also need to: meet college prerequisites, pass placement exams, complete the Lone Star College-CyFair exceptional admissions process, and get campus Dual Credit team approval.

To enroll in Dual Credit English III (ENGL 1301), you must have passed the English II End-of-Course (EOC) assessment. This is a specific additional requirement on top of the standard dual credit eligibility criteria.

For Workforce Dual Credit courses (trades, CTE-based college courses), the eligibility requirement is stricter: you need an overall average of at least 80 in all courses, OR at least 80 in the last course taken in that subject area. The standard 85/75/Masters criteria applies to academic dual credit.

Lone Star College may waive all or part of tuition and required fees for CFISD students in dual credit courses. Students are responsible for any remaining required fees and textbook costs. Students taking dual credit in the summer are responsible for all textbook costs and may need to satisfy bacterial meningitis requirements.

keywords: end of course us history dc
handbookQA.answer: Students enrolling in Dual Credit U.S. History will take the U.S. History End-of-Course (EOC) assessment the following December.
8-week and mini-mester courses offered at Lone Star College throughout the school year are NOT approved dual credit options for CFISD students. Only full-semester courses qualify.

CFISD uses a weighted GPA scale. For Classes through 2029: A in K/AP/HORIZONS = 7 pts, on-level A = 6 pts, below-level A = 5 pts, LIFE Skills A = 4 pts. For Class of 2030+, a new 5-column scale is used: AP/Dual Credit A = 7, K-level (Advanced) A = 6.5, on-level A = 6, below-level A = 5, LIFE Skills A = 4. Semester grade = (3/7 × GP1) + (3/7 × GP2) + (1/7 × Semester Exam).

Class rank is determined by GPA. All high school courses count — including dual credit, summer school, correspondence, night school, and credit-by-exam — EXCEPT student assistant courses, local credit courses, and pass/fail courses. GPA and class rank are calculated each summer after 9th and 10th grade. Estimated rankings are produced at the end of junior year and first semester of senior year for college applications.

Your semester grade is calculated as: (3/7 × Grading Period 1 average) + (3/7 × Grading Period 2 average) + (1/7 × Semester Exam score). This means the semester exam counts for about 14% of your grade and each grading period counts for about 43%.

Only 4 math and 4 science courses count in your GPA calculation. If you took Algebra I in 8th grade and take 4 more math courses in grades 9–12, the 8th-grade Algebra I does NOT count in GPA — the 4 high school math courses do. But if you took Algebra I in 8th grade and only take 3 more math courses in high school, then the 8th-grade Algebra I DOES get included. Algebra I always earns on-level grade points regardless of when taken.

At graduation, three honor designations are awarded: Summa Cum Laude (6.5 GPA or higher), Magna Cum Laude (6.25 GPA or higher), and Cum Laude (6.0 GPA or higher). The final GPA is calculated at the end of senior year. Separately, during the school year, the honor roll has two levels: Distinguished Honor Roll (all 90s) and Regular Honor Roll (majority 90s, rest 80–89), with a conduct grade of at least S required.

Course requests for the following year must be submitted in writing by the last day of April. Once the school year starts, changes are only allowed in the first 2 weeks of each semester, and only for specific reasons: you don't meet the prerequisite, you already have the credit, you're in the wrong level, or there's a scheduling conflict. No course changes are allowed after the 2nd week except for rare district-policy exceptions involving AP/K-level level changes.

keywords: how many credits to be a senior
handbookQA.answer: Grade classification: 9th grade = promotion from middle school. 10th grade = 1 year attendance + 5 credits (must include English I and Algebra I). 11th grade = 2 years attendance + 11 credits. 12th grade = 3 years attendance + 17 credits, or an approved early graduation plan.

You can earn credit through Credit-by-Exam (CBE). Without prior instruction (original credit): you must score 80 or higher. With prior instruction (you've already studied the material elsewhere): you must score 70 or higher, and a fee is charged. CBE credits appear on your transcript and count in GPA. You cannot take a CBE for a course you are currently enrolled in that same semester.

keywords: can i take a course pass fail
handbookQA.answer: 11th and 12th graders may take up to 1 extra course per year on a pass/fail basis (1 as a junior, 1 as a senior). These must be courses beyond the 26 required for graduation, and only certain district-designated courses qualify. You must declare pass/fail intent within the first 2 weeks of the semester. P or F appears on your transcript. Pass/fail grades do NOT count in GPA or class rank, but your actual numerical grade still determines UIL eligibility, honor roll, NHS, and other activity eligibility.
handbookQA.source: Advanced Courses on a Pass/Fail Basis (p. 19)

handbookQA.answer: You may earn up to 2 correspondence learning credits toward graduation. You must get counselor approval before enrolling, have completed at least one semester of 9th grade, maintain a 75 overall GPA, and have a 75 average in a similar prior course. Only courses from UT Austin or Texas Tech University are recognized by TEA. All correspondence grades count in your GPA. Seniors must complete correspondence courses and have grades reported before the 16th week of the fall semester — after that deadline, the course shows as WD (withdrawn) on your transcript and counts against GPA.

You can graduate early in 3 ways: (1) June after 3 complete years of high school (36 months), (2) the summer after 3 years (38 months), or (3) December of your 4th year (43 months — you can still walk in spring graduation). You must file a Declaration of Intent to Graduate Early, signed by a parent, with your counselor at least one semester before your intended graduation date.

To participate in commencement (the graduation ceremony), you must have earned at least 22 credits in designated courses AND passed all 5 required state EOC assessments (English I, English II, Algebra I, Biology, U.S. History).

You must pass 5 End-of-Course (EOC) STAAR assessments to graduate: English I, English II, Algebra I, Biology, and U.S. History. You take each EOC during the school year you are enrolled in that course. You cannot retake a passed EOC. EOC scores do not affect your course grade.
handbookQA.source: Testing Requirements for High School Graduation (p. 31)

handbookQA.answer: CFISD offers both original credit and make-up credit courses each summer. Summer school credits always earn on-level grade points only — even if you're otherwise enrolled in K-level or AP courses during the regular school year.

The Texas Virtual School Network (TxVSN) lets you take online courses for grades 9–12. Courses must match your graduation plan and be counselor-approved. You may take only 1 TxVSN course per semester. All TxVSN courses appear on your transcript and count in GPA. Fees vary and are your responsibility.

CFISD launched Virtual Pathways in 2026–27 with three options: (1) Virtual Academy — fully online, primarily asynchronous, for grades 9–12, students stay enrolled at their home campus. (2) Flex Learning — hybrid for 11th–12th graders, mostly on campus but 1–2 classes online, can arrive late or leave early. (3) Supplemental Courses — tuition-based courses taken outside the school day for acceleration, credit recovery, or extra electives (grades 9–12). All Virtual Pathways courses count in GPA.

Every CFISD student pursues one of 5 endorsements that appear on their diploma: STEM, Business & Industry, Public Services, Arts & Humanities, or Multidisciplinary Studies. An endorsement adds 4 credits beyond the 22-credit Foundation plan (1 advanced math, 1 advanced science, 2 electives) and focuses your course pathway. You select an endorsement during registration and can change it with counselor help.

The STEM endorsement requires Algebra II, Chemistry, and Physics regardless of route. Five options: (1) Computer Science — 4 CS courses including CS I K, AP CSP, CS II K, CS III K; (2) CTE Engineering — 4 CTE credits in STEM cluster with 1 advanced; (3) Math — Algebra II + 2 Algebra-II-prereq courses; (4) Science — Biology + Chem + Physics + 2 advanced sciences from an approved list; (5) Combination — Algebra II + Chem + Physics + 1 extra math + 1 extra science + 3 CS/CTE credits.

The Business & Industry endorsement has 3 options: (1) CTE Sequence — 4 credits in an approved cluster (Ag, Architecture, Arts/A-V, Business, Hospitality, IT, Manufacturing, Transportation) with at least 1 advanced course; (2) Journalism/Debate — 4 English elective credits with 3 levels in Advanced Journalism or Debate; (3) Combination — a coherent 4-credit sequence from options 1 and 2 with at least 1 advanced CTE course.

The Public Services endorsement has 2 options: (1) CTE — 4 credits in Education & Training, Health Science, or Human Services cluster with at least 1 advanced course (3rd year or higher); (2) AFJROTC — 4 AFJROTC courses.

The Arts & Humanities endorsement has 3 options: (1) Social Studies — 5 social studies credits; (2) Languages — 4 levels of the same foreign language, OR 2 levels each in 2 different languages; (3) Fine Arts — 4 courses in the same fine arts area, OR 2 courses each in 2 different fine arts areas.

The Multidisciplinary Studies endorsement has 2 options: (1) 4x4 — 4 English (including English IV) + 4 Math + 4 Science (Biology + Chem and/or Physics) + 4 Social Studies; (2) AP/Dual Credit — 4 AP or Dual Credit courses (or a combination) in English, math, science, social studies, foreign language, or fine arts.

Computer Science I K is available in grades 9–12. Prerequisites: Algebra I. It satisfies the LOTE (Language Other Than English) graduation requirement. It also earns dual college credit through Lone Star College-CyFair (COSC 1301 fall + COSC 1315 spring, 3 college credit hours each semester).

Computer Science II K is available in grades 10–12 (9th graders may enroll concurrently with Algebra II). Prerequisites: CS I K AND Algebra II (or concurrent enrollment). Also satisfies LOTE. Earns dual credit: COSC 1436 fall + COSC 1437 spring (4 college credit hours each semester).
AP Computer Science Principles is available in grades 9–12. Prerequisite: Algebra I. It is recommended to take it BEFORE or CONCURRENTLY with CS II K, and may NOT be taken after CS III K.

You can earn Performance Acknowledgments on your diploma/transcript for outstanding achievement in: (1) Dual Credit — 12+ college credit hours with A or B grades; (2) Bilingual/Bi-literacy — completing English requirements with 80+ AND meeting foreign language proficiency criteria; (3) AP exam — score of 3 or higher; (4) PSAT/SAT/ACT — PSAT commended scholar, SAT 1350+ combined, or ACT composite 29+; (5) Nationally/internationally recognized industry certification.

CFISD has articulation agreements with Lone Star College System and Houston Community College System. Students who complete designated high school courses with qualifying grades and later enroll in a specified college program may receive college credit hours or advanced standing — allowing them to take higher-level college courses. The current approved course list is on the Lone Star College website.

New CFISD students receive credit for all transcripted high school courses from their previous school. However, how those credits count toward GPA and class rank follows CFISD's own GPA structure — they may be included or excluded depending on how they align with CFISD's classification system. Credits from accredited private schools are accepted by transcript. Credits from unaccredited private schools or home schools require credit-by-exam to be awarded.

HORIZONS is CFISD's program for students identified as gifted and talented. Parents can refer their child for screening annually during the Open Referral Period (October 1 through the last school day in November) via the CFISD Parent Portal. HORIZONS courses carry the same grade point weighting as K-level and AP courses. The K-level/Academic Advanced entry/exit criteria also apply to HORIZONS students in cluster classes.

Career and Technical Education (CTE) courses are organized into industry clusters — Agriculture, Architecture, Arts/A-V/Communication, Business/Marketing/Finance, Education, Health Science, Hospitality, IT, Manufacturing, Transportation. To earn an endorsement through CTE, you typically need 4 credits in a cluster with at least 1 advanced course (3rd year or higher in the sequence). Practicum courses for juniors and seniors (16+ years old) may involve off-campus instruction and require your own transportation.

Fully virtual students (CFISD Virtual Academy) can earn the following endorsements in 2026–27: Multidisciplinary Studies (4x4 route), STEM via Computer Science (4 CS courses), STEM via CTE (Engineering program of study), STEM via Math, Business & Industry via Architecture program of study, Arts & Humanities via 5 Social Studies credits, Arts & Humanities via 4 Spanish (or 2 Spanish + 2 of another language).

The best endorsement depends on your interests and career goals. Use the 'Find My Path' tab in this app to match your interests to an endorsement. Multidisciplinary Studies is the most flexible — it keeps all college doors open. STEM suits students interested in technology, engineering, science, or math. You can change your endorsement with counselor help, and sophomore year is the best time to make that switch before it affects junior-year course availability.

K-level (also called Academic Advanced) courses extend grade-level learning and prepare you for future advanced coursework. AP (Advanced Placement) courses go beyond grade-level and can earn you college credit if you score 3 or higher on the AP exam. HORIZONS is CFISD's gifted/talented program, with the same grade point weighting as K-level/AP. All three have the same entry criteria (85+ average or Masters on STAAR/EOC) and exit criteria (74 or below leads to removal).

AP courses are most valuable when you're genuinely interested in the subject and have met the prerequisites with strong grades. Passing the AP exam (score of 3+) can earn college credit and earn a Performance Acknowledgment on your transcript. However, a 74 or lower semester average gets you removed. Balance rigor with realistic performance — a strong grade in an on-level or K-level class is better for GPA and class rank than a weak grade in AP.

Your Bridgeland High School counselor is your best resource for course selection, graduation audits, dual credit enrollment, endorsement changes, and personal circumstances. See the counselor contact information below. For schedule changes, contact the counselor's office before August 1 if you attended summer school or completed a correspondence course.

8.focus: Use 8th grade to understand your interests, review high school sequencing, and avoid closing doors before freshman year starts. Decisions now — especially in math and language — can significantly expand or limit your options later.

9.stage: Build Foundation and Keep Doors Open
9.focus: Freshman year should cover required basics while starting a pathway sequence that does not close future options. Every course in 9th grade creates a prerequisite chain — choose courses that open the next door, not just fill a slot.
checklist: Complete PACE (½ credit) — required for all 9th graders; PACE Plus (1 credit) required for some based on 8th grade performance
Enroll in English I, the appropriate math course, Biology, and a social studies course
Start endorsement-aligned electives or an intro CTE / Computer Science course
Track K/AP performance carefully — a 74 or lower semester average triggers removal from the advanced level
Confirm whether Algebra II is part of your long-term plan (needed for Distinguished Level of Achievement)
Meet with your counselor to confirm your 4-year plan and endorsement direction
milestones: Complete PACE or PACE Plus (grade 9 requirement)

11.stage: Go Deep and Use Advanced Options Strategically
11.focus: Junior year is where transcripts become specialized and postsecondary alignment matters most. Use AP and Dual Credit carefully — only where readiness is strong and prerequisites are genuinely met. A challenging schedule with strong grades beats an overloaded one with poor performance.
checklist: Use AP or Dual Credit only where readiness is strong and all prerequisites are confirmed
Deepen your pathway with advanced or practicum-level courses where available
Review class rank, GPA weighting, and endorsement completion status before spring registration

12.focus: Senior year should close all credit gaps, complete endorsement requirements, and avoid last-minute surprises. This is not the year for experimentation — it's the year for clean execution. Verify everything with your counselor before November.
